disagreements.topic: How much can automated accessibility testing cover?

positions.position: 57.38% of issues by volume (Deque, vendor dataset); Deque also concedes only 16/50 WCAG 2.1 AA SC show automated issues.
At most 50% SC coverage, 14-38% completeness, 66-71% correctness (peer-reviewed measurement, 2013).
axe-core + PA11Y combined find around 35% of issues (UK DWP guidance).
W3C says automated checks are non-definitive and require human judgment; Lighthouse excludes manual audits from its score.

disagreements.note: The numbers are not directly comparable because denominators differ (issues vs success criteria vs problems) and the datasets differ; Deque explicitly reframes the denominator. Reported as a live disagreement rather than averaged.

disagreements.topic: Does JavaScript rendering 'just work' for search engines?

positions.position: Google documents a functioning crawl/render/index pipeline using headless Chromium and indexes rendered HTML.

The same official docs warn that not all bots run JS, recommend SSR/prerendering, and list WRS limits (state cleared each load, caches ignored, no WebGL/WebSocket/WebRTC, permission prompts declined).
Third-party SEO articles go further (e.g. claims that 'Googlebot can't click'), but those interaction claims were not found in the official pages retrieved here.

disagreements.note: Tension between official reassurance and official caveats; SSR-vendor style claims were not verified as sources and are excluded.

disagreements.topic: Is accessibility risk concentrated in what automation cannot see?

positions.position: Over-reliance on automated tests is measurably harmful; half of success criteria are never even analyzed.
Automation catches a majority of real issues by volume and the 20-30% 'belief' is based on the wrong metric.
W3C's check-by-check guidance repeatedly requires human judgment (alt-text appropriateness, keyboard flows, focus visibility).

disagreements.note: Vendor framing versus independent measurement versus standards guidance; unresolved.

disagreements.topic: Browser-based network inspection also has blind spots.

positions.position: Playwright documents that service workers can make requests invisible to page.route/browserContext.route unless serviceWorkers:'block' is set.
Playwright MCP's own origin allow/deny lists 'do not serve as a security boundary'.
Execution shows the complementary blind spot: a server-side fetch never sees the XHR the page would issue (server log: GET / only).

disagreements.note: Neither mode gives a complete network picture.

disagreements.topic: Observation modality for agent-native browsers disagrees across vendors.

positions.position: Playwright MCP defaults to accessibility-tree snapshots and says screenshots cannot be used to act ('bypassing the need for screenshots'). Vision input is opt-in (--caps=vision).
Chrome DevTools MCP provides both a11y snapshots and DevTools-grade traces/Lighthouse/emulation, positioning itself as the inspection surface.

disagreements.note: A token/latency-versus-fidelity trade-off; Microsoft's README additionally warns MCP tool schemas and snapshots consume model context.
